chapters.title: Project 1: projectile motion
chapters.what: Vectors, trigonometry, calculus, Newton's laws, energy and numerical integration meet in one problem: launch a ball and predict where it lands, with and without air resistance.
chapters.looks: The trajectory with velocity and acceleration arrows (2D); the 3D flight with crosswind and spin (3D).
chapters.change: Add drag: the range shrinks and the best angle drops below 45°.
chapters.use: Sports, ballistics, fountains, space launches, games.
misc: The horizontal velocity is constant only without drag.
At the top the velocity is not zero, only its vertical part.

examples.title: Range in a vacuum
examples.world: v₀ = 20 m/s at 45°: R = v₀²/g = 40.8 m.

examples.title: Maximum height
examples.world: The peak is at v₀² sin²θ/2g = 10.2 m.

examples.title: Flight time
examples.world: T = 2v₀ sin θ/g = 2.88 s.

examples.title: Complementary angles
examples.world: 30° and 60° give the same range, 35.3 m.

examples.title: From a cliff
examples.world: Launched from 20 m up the ball flies 55.5 m.

examples.title: Quadratic drag
examples.world: A baseball-like drag cuts the range and makes the path asymmetric.

chapters.title: Project 3: double pendulum
chapters.what: Vectors, rotation, Lagrangian mechanics, nonlinear ODEs and chaos: two linked pendulums are the simplest mechanical system with sensitive dependence on initial conditions.
chapters.looks: The motion and its angles (2D); the trajectory (3D).
chapters.change: Change the release angle by 0.1°: after a few seconds the motions no longer agree.
chapters.use: Robot arms, cranes with hanging loads, human gait, chaos theory.
misc: Chaotic does not mean random: the equations are deterministic.
Small swings are not chaotic: they are a sum of two normal modes.

examples.title: Chaos in a double pendulum
examples.world: Shinbrot et al. (1992) measured the exponential divergence of nearby motions.

examples.title: Sensitivity to initial conditions
examples.world: Change θ₀ by 0.1° and compare after 10 s.

examples.title: Small swings are regular
examples.world: At 5° the motion is a superposition of two normal modes.

examples.title: The single pendulum's phase space
examples.world: A 2 rad release: the leapfrog period matches 2π/(ω₀ AGM(1, cos 1)).

examples.title: Energy as a check on the integrator
examples.world: E = −cos 2 = 0.416 must stay constant; its drift measures numerical error.

chapters.title: Project 4: heat diffusion
chapters.what: Calculus, PDEs, numerics and thermodynamics: temperature spreads by u_t = αu_xx; in steady state it satisfies Laplace's or Poisson's equation, solvable by finite differences or finite elements.
chapters.looks: Temperature profiles and fields (2D); the temperature surface over space and time (3D).
chapters.change: Raise r above ½: the explicit scheme blows up.
chapters.use: Electronics cooling, building insulation, cooking, geothermal wells.
misc: Heat flux is driven by the gradient, not the temperature.
A stable scheme can still be inaccurate.

examples.title: Cooling of a rod: exact decay e^{−απ²t}
examples.world: A sine profile keeps its shape and decays exponentially (Fourier's solution).

examples.title: The stability limit r ≤ ½
examples.world: At r = 0.6 the explicit scheme produces growing wiggles.

examples.title: A plate with one hot edge
examples.world: Steady conduction: the centre sits at 25 by symmetry.

examples.title: Internal heating by finite elements
examples.world: A uniformly heated square plate with cold edges (FEM).

examples.title: Heat loss through a wall
examples.world: Brick–insulation–brick with 21 °C inside and −5 °C outside: q = ΔT/ΣR = 10.6 W/m².

chapters.title: Project 5: fluid through a pipe
chapters.what: Continuity, momentum, energy, the Reynolds number and pressure loss: the flow in a pipe is laminar (parabolic profile) at low Re and turbulent with a flatter profile at high Re.
chapters.looks: The velocity profile and pressure line (2D); the 3D velocity profile in the pipe (3D).
chapters.change: Raise the speed through Re ≈ 2300: the profile flattens and the friction jumps.
chapters.use: Water mains, oil pipelines, blood vessels, HVAC ducts.
misc: Doubling the flow more than doubles the pressure drop in turbulent flow.
Laminar friction does not depend on roughness.

examples.title: Reynolds' transition
examples.world: Reynolds (1883) saw dye streaks break up near Re ≈ 2300.

examples.title: Laminar friction factor 64/Re
examples.world: Hagen–Poiseuille flow at Re = 500.

examples.title: The parabolic profile
examples.world: In laminar flow the centre-line speed is twice the mean.

examples.title: Turbulent pressure drop (Colebrook)
examples.world: 100 m of 5 cm commercial steel pipe at 1 m/s loses 23.7 kPa.

examples.title: A turbulent water main
examples.world: Re = 50 000: fully turbulent.

chapters.title: Project 8: quantum particle in a box
chapters.what: Complex numbers, differential equations, linear algebra, probability and quantum mechanics: confine a particle and its energy is quantised; superpositions slosh back and forth in time.
chapters.looks: Energy levels and wavefunctions (2D); |Ψ(x, t)|² of a superposition over time (3D).
chapters.change: Narrow the box: all levels rise as 1/a².
chapters.use: Quantum dots, conjugated dyes, nanowires, semiconductor lasers.
misc: The particle does not bounce between the walls like a ball.
|ψ|² is a probability density, not a charge cloud of many particles.

examples.title: Ground-state energy
examples.world: E₁ = π² in units ħ = 2m = 1.

examples.title: Levels grow as n²
examples.world: E₂/E₁ = 4.

examples.title: A superposition sloshes
examples.world: Mixing n = 1 and 2 makes |Ψ|² oscillate at (E₂ − E₁)/h (see the 3D view).

examples.title: Quantum dots: size sets colour
examples.world: Halve the size, quadruple the energy (Brus 1984).

examples.title: Compare: the harmonic oscillator
examples.world: Unlike the box, its levels are evenly spaced.
